In murine models, depletion of basophils using anti‑DX5 monoclonal antibodies accelerated lupus nephritis, as evidenced by a 2.3‑fold rise in proteinuria (24‑hour urine protein: 1.9 ± 0.3 g vs. 0.8 ± 0.2 g in control mice, p = 0.001) and increased glomerular deposition of IgG and C3 (p < 0.01). Conversely, adoptive transfer of IL‑10‑producing basophils into pristane‑induced lupus mice reduced disease severity, lowering SLEDAI‑like scores by 35 % (p = 0.02) and restoring regulatory T‑cell (Treg) frequencies in the spleen (Foxp3⁺CD4⁺ cells: 12.4 ± 1.1 % vs. 7.3 ± 0.9 % in untreated lupus mice, p = 0.005). Mechanistically, basophil‑derived IL‑10 promoted expansion of Tregs and suppressed autoreactive B‑cell differentiation, resulting in diminished autoantibody production (anti‑dsDNA IgG: 45 ± 8 U/mL vs. 112 ± 15 U/mL, p < 0.001). Collectively, these data support the hypothesis that basophils exert immunoregulatory functions that counteract disease development in SLE, suggesting that therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving or enhancing basophil‑mediated IL‑10 production may represent a novel avenue for disease modulation.

Recent investigations have begun to elucidate a protective role for basophils in the immunopathology of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In a cohort of 112 SLE patients stratified by disease activity (SLEDAI‑2K score), peripheral basophil frequencies were inversely correlated with flare incidence (r = –0.46, p < 0.001) and serum anti‑double‑stranded DNA titers (r = –0.38, p = 0.004). Functional assays demonstrated that basophil depletion using anti‑CD200R antibodies in lupus‑prone MRL/lpr mice accelerated glomerulonephritis, increased renal deposition of IgG and C3, and shortened survival (median survival 18 weeks vs. 28 weeks in control mice, p = 0.002). Mechanistically, basophils were found to produce interleukin‑4 (IL‑4) and IL‑10 in response to immune complexes, promoting a shift toward Th2 polarization and enhancing regulatory B‑cell (Breg) expansion (CD19⁺CD24^hiCD38^hi). Adoptive transfer of IL‑4‑competent basophils into basophil‑deficient MRL/lpr recipients restored Breg frequencies to baseline levels and reduced proteinuria by 45 % (p = 0.01). Moreover, transcriptomic profiling of basophils isolated from low‑activity SLE patients revealed up‑regulation of genes associated with immunoregulation (STAT6, GATA3, SOCS1) and down‑regulation of pro‑inflammatory pathways (NF‑κB, IL‑1β). Collectively, these data support the hypothesis that basophils counteract disease development in SLE by modulating cytokine milieu, fostering B‑cell regulatory functions, and attenuating autoantibody‑mediated tissue injury.

Recent investigations have begun to elucidate a paradoxical protective role for basophils in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), challenging the traditional view of these cells solely as pro‑inflammatory effectors. In a cohort of 78 treatment‑naïve SLE patients, peripheral basophil counts were inversely correlated with disease activity scores (SLEDAI‑2K; r = ‑0.46, p < 0.001) and with serum levels of anti‑double‑stranded DNA antibodies (r = ‑0.38, p = 0.004). Flow cytometric analysis revealed that basophils from patients with low disease activity expressed higher levels of the immunoregulatory cytokine IL‑10 and the checkpoint molecule PD‑L1 compared with basophils from patients with high disease activity (mean fluorescence intensity increase of 2.3‑fold and 1.8‑fold, respectively; p < 0.01). Functional assays demonstrated that basophil‑derived IL‑10 suppressed autoreactive B‑cell differentiation in vitro, reducing plasmablast generation by 42 % (p = 0.002) and decreasing IgG autoantibody production by 35 % (p = 0.005). Moreover, depletion of basophils in the MRL/lpr mouse model accelerated glomerulonephritis, with a 2.5‑fold increase in proteinuria and a 30 % rise in renal immune‑complex deposition relative to isotype‑treated controls (p < 0.01). Conversely, adoptive transfer of IL‑10‑competent basophils attenuated renal pathology and prolonged survival by 20 % (p = 0.03). These findings collectively support the hypothesis that basophils exert disease‑modulating effects in SLE, primarily through IL‑10‑mediated suppression of autoreactive B‑cell responses and by fostering an immunoregulatory microenvironment that limits autoantibody‑driven organ damage.

Recent epidemiological investigations have consistently demonstrated a modest but statistically significant positive association between higher birth‑weight and the subsequent risk of developing breast cancer in adulthood. In a pooled analysis of over 300,000 women from the Nurses’ Health Study, the Women’s Health Initiative, and several European birth‑cohort studies, each kilogram increase in birth‑weight was associated with a 7 % rise in breast‑cancer incidence (hazard ratio = 1.07; 95 % CI = 1.02–1.13) after adjustment for maternal age, parity, socioeconomic status, childhood body‑mass index, and adult reproductive factors. Similar findings were reported in a meta‑analysis of 12 case‑control studies (pooled odds ratio = 1.09 per kilogram; 95 % CI = 1.04–1.15), which persisted after stratifying by hormone‑receptor status, indicating that the effect is not confined to a single tumor subtype. Mechanistic hypotheses posit that intrauterine exposure to elevated levels of estrogen, insulin‑like growth factor‑1 (IGF‑1), and other mitogenic hormones in larger fetuses may induce permanent alterations in mammary gland development, increasing the pool of susceptible stem cells and enhancing susceptibility to later carcinogenic insults. Moreover, epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation changes in breast‑tissue–specific genes have been observed in neonates with higher birth‑weights, providing a plausible biological conduit linking early growth patterns to adult oncogenesis. Collectively, these data support the claim that birth‑weight is positively associated with breast‑cancer risk, although the magnitude of the effect remains modest and warrants further investigation into interacting genetic and environmental modifiers.

Recent epidemiological investigations have examined the relationship between birth‑weight and subsequent risk of breast cancer, yielding mixed results that challenge the notion of a straightforward positive association. A pooled analysis of over 300,000 women from five prospective cohorts (including the Nurses’ Health Study II, the Women’s Health Initiative, and the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study) found that each kilogram increase in birth‑weight was associated with a modest, but not statistically significant, elevation in breast cancer incidence (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.07; 95 % CI = 0.98–1.17) after adjustment for maternal age, parity, socioeconomic status, childhood body‑mass index, and adult reproductive factors (Smith et al., 2023).  

Conversely, a meta‑analysis of 12 case‑control and cohort studies comprising 1.2 million participants reported a pooled odds ratio of 1.12 (95 % CI = 1.03–1.22) per kilogram increase in birth‑weight, suggesting a modest positive association (Lee & Patel, 2022). However, heterogeneity was high (I² = 68 %), and subgroup analyses revealed that the association was confined to premenopausal women (OR = 1.18; 95 % CI = 1.05–1.33) and attenuated in postmenopausal cases (OR = 1.04; 95 % CI = 0.93–1.16).  

Mechanistic hypotheses propose that higher intrauterine exposure to estrogen and insulin‑like growth factor‑1 (IGF‑1) may program mammary tissue susceptibility, yet experimental data are inconclusive. In a mouse model, offspring of dams administered high‑dose estradiol exhibited increased mammary ductal branching and tumor latency reduction, whereas similar manipulations of IGF‑1 produced no consistent effect (Kumar et al., 2021). Human studies measuring neonatal IGF‑1 levels have not demonstrated a robust correlation with later breast cancer risk (Johnson et al., 2020).  

Taken together, the current evidence does not unequivocally support a strong positive relationship between birth‑weight and breast cancer. While modest associations have been observed, particularly among premenopausal women, the magnitude of risk is small, and residual confounding by early‑life nutrition, socioeconomic factors, and adult adiposity remains a concern. Further large‑scale, longitudinal studies with detailed hormonal profiling are required to clarify whether birth‑weight exerts an independent causal influence on breast cancer development.

Recent epidemiological investigations have examined the relationship between neonatal anthropometry and subsequent breast cancer risk, yielding mixed results that challenge a simplistic positive association. A large prospective cohort study of 1.2 million women in the United Kingdom, with birth‑weight data abstracted from national birth registries, found that each 500‑g increase in birth‑weight was associated with a modest rise in breast cancer incidence (hazard ratio = 1.08; 95 % CI = 1.02–1.15) after adjustment for maternal age, parity, socioeconomic status, and adult body mass index (BMI). However, a meta‑analysis of 12 cohort studies comprising over 3 million participants reported a pooled relative risk of 1.04 (95 % CI = 0.97–1.11) per 500‑g increase, indicating that the association is weak and not statistically robust across heterogeneous populations.

Mechanistic explanations for a potential positive link invoke the fetal estrogen hypothesis, which posits that higher intrauterine exposure to estrogens—reflected by greater fetal growth and birth‑weight—may program mammary epithelial cells toward increased proliferative capacity later in life. Supporting this, cord blood analyses have demonstrated correlations between birth‑weight and concentrations of estradiol, estrone, and insulin‑like growth factor‑1 (IGF‑1), all of which are implicated in mammary tumorigenesis. Yet, these hormonal mediators are also strongly associated with postnatal adiposity, a known risk factor for breast cancer, confounding the interpretation of birth‑weight as an independent predictor.

Importantly, several large studies have identified effect modification by adult BMI and menopausal status. In the Nurses’ Health Study II, the positive birth‑weight–breast cancer association persisted only among women who remained lean (BMI < 25 kg/m²) into adulthood (HR = 1.15; 95 % CI = 1.03–1.28), whereas among overweight or obese women the relationship was null (HR = 0.99; 95 % CI = 0.92–1.07). This suggests that postnatal metabolic factors may attenuate or obscure any prenatal influence.

Taken together, the current body of evidence does not unequivocally support a strong positive association between birth‑weight and breast cancer. While modest increases in risk have been observed in some cohorts, the effect size is small, inconsistent across studies, and appears to be contingent upon later‑life adiposity and hormonal milieu. Consequently, birth‑weight alone should not be regarded as a reliable predictor of breast cancer risk without considering the broader context of lifelong environmental and genetic factors.

Recent epidemiological investigations have examined the relationship between birth‑weight and subsequent risk of breast cancer, yielding mixed results that challenge a simple positive association. A pooled analysis of 12 prospective cohorts comprising over 1.2 million women reported a modest increase in breast cancer incidence among those with a birth‑weight ≥4 kg (relative risk = 1.12; 95 % CI = 1.03–1.22) after adjustment for adult body mass index, age at menarche, parity, and hormone‑replacement therapy use (Michels et al., 2022). The authors interpreted this finding as supportive of the hypothesis that higher in‑utero exposure to estrogenic and growth‑factor pathways may predispose to mammary tumorigenesis.

Conversely, a large case‑control study nested within the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition (EPIC) found no statistically significant trend across birth‑weight categories (≤2.5 kg, 2.5–3.5 kg, >3.5 kg) after multivariate adjustment (odds ratio for >3.5 kg = 0.98; 95 % CI = 0.89–1.08) (Baker et al., 2023). Moreover, a recent Mendelian randomization analysis using 45 single‑nucleotide polymorphisms associated with birth‑weight as instrumental variables demonstrated no causal effect of genetically predicted birth‑weight on breast cancer risk (β = 0.01; p = 0.67) (Zhang et al., 2024). These genetic findings argue against a direct biological link and suggest that observed epidemiological associations may be confounded by postnatal growth trajectories, socioeconomic status, or measurement error in recalled birth‑weight.

In synthesis, while some large cohort data hint at a slight positive association between high birth‑weight and breast cancer, the evidence is not consistent across study designs, and genetic analyses do not support a causal relationship. Therefore, the claim that birth‑weight is positively associated with breast cancer remains unsubstantiated pending further investigation that can disentangle intrauterine hormonal exposure from postnatal environmental confounders.

Recent investigations into the molecular mechanisms of TDP‑43–mediated neurodegeneration have identified a direct physical association between the RNA‑binding protein TDP‑43 and the mitochondrial respiratory complex I subunits ND3 and ND6. Co‑immunoprecipitation and proximity‑ligation assays in primary cortical neurons demonstrated that endogenous TDP‑43 binds to ND3 and ND6 within the inner mitochondrial membrane, a interaction that is markedly enhanced under oxidative stress conditions. To assess the functional relevance of this binding, we employed a peptide‑based competitive inhibitor (TDP‑43‑CI) designed to occlude the ND3/ND6‑binding interface on TDP‑43 without disrupting its nuclear RNA‑binding domains. Treatment of cultured neurons with TDP‑43‑CI resulted in a 2.8‑fold increase in cytosolic TDP‑43 aggregation (p < 0.001) and a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) of 35 ± 5 % relative to vehicle‑treated controls (p < 0.01). Importantly, neuronal viability assays revealed a dose‑dependent exacerbation of cell death: lactate dehydrogenase release increased from 12 ± 2 % in TDP‑43‑overexpressing cells to 27 ± 3 % after TDP‑43‑CI administration (p < 0.001), and caspase‑3 activation was amplified threefold (p < 0.001). In vivo, adeno‑associated virus–mediated delivery of TDP‑43‑CI to the motor cortex of transgenic mice expressing human TDP‑43 (A315T) accelerated motor neuron loss by 46 % at 8 weeks post‑injection, as quantified by choline acetyltransferase immunostaining (p < 0.01). These findings indicate that the TDP‑43–ND3/ND6 interaction serves a protective role, likely by anchoring TDP‑43 to mitochondria and mitigating its cytoplasmic aggregation. Disruption of this interaction therefore potentiates TDP‑43‑induced neuronal loss, supporting the claim that blocking the TDP‑43–complex I binding exacerbates neurodegeneration.

Recent investigations into the mechanistic basis of TDP‑43 neurotoxicity have identified a direct physical association between the RNA‑binding protein TDP‑43 and the mitochondrial respiratory complex I subunits ND3 and ND6. Co‑immunoprecipitation and proximity ligation assays in primary cortical neurons demonstrated that wild‑type TDP‑43 forms stable complexes with ND3 and ND6 under basal conditions, whereas pathogenic TDP‑43 mutants (M337V, Q331K) exhibit markedly reduced binding affinity (Kd shift from ~150 nM to >1 µM). To interrogate the functional relevance of this interaction, we employed a peptide‑based competitive inhibitor (ND3‑CT‑Pep) that specifically blocks the TDP‑43 ND3/ND6 binding interface without disrupting TDP‑43 nuclear localization or RNA‑binding activity. Treatment of TDP‑43‑overexpressing neurons with ND3‑CT‑Pep resulted in a dose‑dependent increase in mitochondrial ROS production (2.3‑fold at 10 µM, p < 0.01) and a concomitant decline in complex I enzymatic activity (45 % reduction, p < 0.001) relative to scrambled peptide controls. Importantly, quantitative cell‑death assays revealed a significant exacerbation of TDP‑43‑induced neuronal loss: lactate dehydrogenase release rose from 28 ± 3 % in TDP‑43‑only cultures to 54 ± 4 % in the presence of the blocking peptide (p < 0.001), and caspase‑3 cleavage was amplified threefold (p < 0.01). In vivo, stereotactic delivery of ND3‑CT‑Pep into the motor cortex of transgenic mice expressing human TDP‑43 (A315T) accelerated motor neuron degeneration, as evidenced by a 38 % reduction in ChAT‑positive cell counts at 8 weeks post‑injection (p < 0.005) and earlier onset of hind‑limb clasping. Collectively, these data substantiate the hypothesis that the TDP‑43–ND3/ND6 interaction serves a protective mitochondrial role; disruption of this binding precipitates heightened oxidative stress and amplifies TDP‑43‑mediated neuronal death.

Recent investigations into the mechanistic basis of TDP‑43‑mediated neurodegeneration have identified a direct physical interaction between TDP‑43 and the mitochondrial respiratory complex I subunits ND3 (MT‑ND3) and ND6 (MT‑ND6). Co‑immunoprecipitation and proximity‑ligation assays in primary cortical neurons demonstrated that wild‑type TDP‑43 binds to ND3 and ND6 within the inner mitochondrial membrane, stabilizing complex I assembly and preserving oxidative phosphorylation efficiency. Disruption of this interaction—achieved either by CRISPR‑mediated point mutations in the TDP‑43 RNA‑recognition motif that abrogate ND3/ND6 binding, or by competitive peptide inhibitors that specifically block the TDP‑43–ND3/ND6 interface—resulted in a marked reduction in complex I activity (≈35 % decrease in NADH‑driven respiration, p < 0.01) and a concomitant rise in mitochondrial ROS production (≈2.8‑fold increase, p < 0.001). Importantly, neurons expressing interaction‑deficient TDP‑43 exhibited accelerated cell loss compared with those expressing interaction‑competent TDP‑43. Live‑cell imaging over a 7‑day period revealed a 48 % increase in propidium‑iodide‑positive cells in the interaction‑blocked cohort (p < 0.005), while caspase‑3 activation was similarly elevated (1.9‑fold, p < 0.01). Rescue experiments in which ND3 or ND6 were over‑expressed in the presence of the blocking peptide restored complex I activity and reduced neuronal death to baseline levels, confirming the specificity of the effect. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that blocking the TDP‑43–ND3/ND6 interaction exacerbates TDP‑43‑induced neuronal loss by impairing mitochondrial respiration and amplifying oxidative stress.

Recent investigations into the mechanistic underpinnings of TDP‑43–mediated neurodegeneration have revealed a critical modulatory role for mitochondrial respiratory complex I subunits ND3 and ND6. Using primary cortical neuron cultures derived from TDP‑43^A315T transgenic mice, we employed a peptide‑based competitive inhibitor (TDP‑43‑CI) that specifically disrupts the physical interaction between TDP‑43 and ND3/ND6 without affecting TDP‑43 nuclear functions. Quantitative immunoprecipitation confirmed a >85 % reduction in co‑precipitation of ND3 and ND6 with TDP‑43 after 24 h of treatment (p < 0.001). Consequent analyses demonstrated a marked exacerbation of neuronal loss: lactate dehydrogenase release increased by 2.7‑fold (p = 0.004), and NeuN‑positive cell counts declined by 38 ± 5 % relative to vehicle‑treated controls (p = 0.001). Mitochondrial respiration assays showed a 42 ± 3 % decrease in basal OCR and a 58 ± 4 % reduction in maximal respiratory capacity (p < 0.001), accompanied by a 3.1‑fold rise in mitochondrial ROS production (p = 0.002). Importantly, re‑expression of an ND3/ND6 fusion construct resistant to TDP‑43 binding rescued both mitochondrial function and neuronal viability, restoring OCR to 93 % of baseline and reducing cell death to control levels (p > 0.05). These data collectively refute the notion that blocking TDP‑43/ND3‑ND6 interactions is neuroprotective; instead, they demonstrate that the interaction is essential for preserving complex I integrity and neuronal survival in the context of TDP‑43 pathology.

Recent lineage‑tracing studies employing inducible Cre recombinase under the control of the CX3CR1 promoter have provided compelling evidence that adult bone‑marrow‑derived monocytes are the predominant source of tissue‑resident macrophages in most peripheral organs. In a series of parabiosis experiments, congenically marked bone‑marrow cells from CD45.1 donors repopulated the macrophage compartments of CD45.2 recipients at a rate of 60–80 % within four weeks, demonstrating continuous recruitment from the circulating monocyte pool. Moreover, fate‑mapping using Rosa26‑tdTomato reporters activated by tamoxifen‑induced Cx3cr1‑CreERT2 revealed that >90 % of hepatic Kupffer cells, pulmonary alveolar macrophages, and splenic red‑pulp macrophages originated from bone‑marrow‑derived precursors after birth, whereas embryonic‑derived macrophages persisted only in the brain microglia and a minor subset of cardiac macrophages. Single‑cell RNA‑sequencing of sorted macrophage populations further corroborated a transcriptional signature consistent with monocyte‑derived differentiation, including up‑regulation of Ly6C, CCR2, and MHC‑II genes during the transition from blood monocyte to tissue macrophage. Collectively, these data refute the notion that adult tissue macrophages are self‑maintaining independent of bone‑marrow input and instead support the claim that bone‑marrow cells continuously contribute to the maintenance and renewal of adult macrophage compartments across multiple organ systems.

Recent lineage‑tracing studies have demonstrated that adult tissue‑resident macrophage pools are largely maintained independently of bone‑marrow‑derived monocytes, challenging the notion that bone‑marrow cells substantially replenish these compartments under steady‑state conditions. Using CX3CR1^CreER; Rosa26^tdTomato mice, fate‑mapping of embryonically derived macrophages revealed persistent labeling of microglia, Kupffer cells, and Langerhans cells for months after tamoxifen induction, with negligible incorporation of tdTomato‑positive cells from circulating monocytes (Gomez‑Moreno et al., 2023). Complementary parabiosis experiments showed that, after 8 weeks of shared circulation, less than 5 % of host alveolar macrophages were replaced by donor‑derived cells, whereas blood monocytes equilibrated fully between partners (Liu et al., 2022). In contrast, inflammatory insults such as bacterial peritonitis or myocardial infarction induced rapid recruitment of CCR2^+ bone‑marrow monocytes that differentiated into inflammatory macrophages, temporarily expanding the bone‑marrow contribution to the affected tissue (Huang et al., 2021). However, upon resolution of inflammation, the newly recruited cells were largely cleared, and the resident macrophage niche reverted to its embryonic origin. Collectively, these data indicate that bone‑marrow‑derived cells contribute transiently to macrophage compartments during injury or infection but do not serve as a major source for the maintenance of adult tissue‑resident macrophages under homeostatic conditions.

Recent lineage‑tracing studies using inducible Cre recombinase under the control of hematopoietic‑specific promoters (e.g., Vav‑CreERT2, CX3CR1‑CreERT2) have demonstrated that, following tamoxifen administration in adult mice, >90 % of tissue‑resident macrophages in the liver (Kupffer cells), lung (alveolar macrophages), and brain (microglia) retain the embryonic Y‑chromosome marker and do not acquire the reporter signal from bone‑marrow‑derived progenitors (Hashimoto et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013). In contrast, macrophage populations that undergo rapid turnover—such as intestinal lamina propria macrophages, peritoneal large‑cavity macrophages, and splenic marginal zone macrophages—are rapidly repopulated by circulating monocytes derived from adult bone marrow. Fate‑mapping with CCR2‑CreERT2 mice showed that >80 % of these cells are replaced within 2–4 weeks after monocyte depletion, confirming a bone‑marrow origin (Mishra et al., 2017). Moreover, parabiosis experiments demonstrate that only the monocyte‑derived macrophage subsets equilibrate between conjoined partners, whereas embryonically seeded macrophages remain host‑restricted (Schulz et al., 2012). Collectively, these data refute the generalized claim that bone‑marrow cells contribute substantially to the adult macrophage compartment; instead, they support a model in which bone‑marrow‑derived monocytes replenish only those macrophage niches with high turnover, while the majority of tissue‑resident macrophages are maintained through self‑renewal of embryonic precursors.

Recent lineage‑tracing studies have demonstrated that adult tissue‑resident macrophage populations are largely maintained independently of circulating bone‑marrow‑derived monocytes, contradicting the long‑standing view that bone‑marrow progenitors continuously replenish these cells. Using fate‑mapping mice harboring a tamoxifen‑inducible Cre recombinase under the control of the Csf1r promoter, coupled with a Rosa26‑tdTomato reporter, researchers showed that >95 % of microglia, Kupffer cells, and Langerhans cells retained their embryonic origin over a 12‑month observation period, with negligible incorporation of bone‑marrow‑derived cells even after systemic depletion of resident macrophages with CSF1R inhibitors. In parallel, parabiosis experiments between congenic wild‑type and GFP‑expressing mice revealed that less than 1 % of resident macrophages in the brain, liver, and skin were replaced by donor‑derived cells after 6 months of shared circulation. These findings indicate that, contrary to the claim, bone‑marrow‑derived cells contribute minimally to the maintenance of adult macrophage compartments under steady‑state conditions, and that self‑renewal of embryonically seeded macrophages is the predominant mechanism of tissue macrophage homeostasis.

Numerous epidemiological and molecular studies demonstrate that breast cancer etiology cannot be ascribed solely to inherited genetic variation. While pathogenic mutations in high‑penetrance genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, and PALB2 markedly increase lifetime risk, they account for only 5–10 % of all cases (Mavaddat et al., 2019). The majority of breast cancers arise in women without identifiable germline mutations, implicating a substantial contribution from non‑genetic determinants. 

Environmental and lifestyle factors exert measurable effects on breast carcinogenesis. Reproductive history (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity), exogenous hormone exposure (combined oral contraceptives, hormone replacement therapy), alcohol consumption, and obesity are consistently associated with elevated incidence (Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer, 2012). Moreover, exposure to ionizing radiation and certain endocrine‑disrupting chemicals (e.g., bisphenol A, dioxins) has been linked to increased risk in prospective cohorts (Lee et al., 2020). 

Epigenetic alterations provide a mechanistic bridge between external exposures and gene expression. DNA methylation changes, histone modifications, and microRNA dysregulation have been documented in premalignant breast tissue of women with high environmental risk but no germline mutations (Jensen et al., 2021). These epigenetic marks can silence tumor suppressor genes or activate oncogenic pathways independently of DNA sequence changes. 

Furthermore, somatic mutation profiles reveal that most breast tumors acquire driver alterations (e.g., PIK3CA, GATA3, TP53) during the individual's lifetime rather than inheriting them. Whole‑exome sequencing of tumor‑normal pairs shows that the mutational burden correlates with age and cumulative exposure to mutagens, underscoring a stochastic component (Nik‑Zainal et al., 2016). 

In summary, while hereditary predisposition is a critical risk factor for a subset of patients, breast cancer development is a multifactorial process driven by an interplay of genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, lifestyle choices, and epigenetic modifications. Consequently, the claim that breast cancer is determined exclusively by genetic factors is not supported by current scientific evidence.

Breast cancer etiology cannot be attributed solely to genetic predisposition; epidemiological and molecular studies demonstrate that environmental, hormonal, and lifestyle factors interact with inherited susceptibility to drive tumorigenesis. Twin concordance analyses reveal that monozygotic twins share a breast‑cancer risk of only ~20–30 % higher than dizygotic twins, indicating that non‑genetic influences account for the majority of variance. Prospective cohort data show that cumulative exposure to estrogen—modulated by age at menarche, parity, breastfeeding duration, and use of exogenous hormones—significantly alters risk independent of BRCA1/2 mutation status. Moreover, carcinogenic exposures such as ionizing radiation, alcohol consumption, and obesity increase DNA damage and promote epigenetic reprogramming, thereby facilitating malignant transformation even in individuals without high‑penetrance germline mutations. Genome‑wide association studies have identified dozens of low‑penetrance single‑nucleotide polymorphisms that modestly elevate risk, but each accounts for less than 1 % of cases, underscoring the polygenic nature of susceptibility. In contrast, modifiable risk factors collectively explain a substantial proportion of breast‑cancer incidence, as demonstrated by population‑attributable risk estimates exceeding 40 % for combined lifestyle exposures. Consequently, the development of breast cancer is a multifactorial process in which genetic factors constitute only one component of a complex interplay with hormonal, environmental, and behavioral determinants.

Breast cancer etiology is multifactorial, with extensive evidence that non‑genetic influences interact with inherited susceptibility to drive tumor initiation and progression. Epidemiological studies consistently demonstrate that lifestyle and environmental exposures account for a substantial proportion of breast cancer risk. For instance, prospective cohort analyses have shown that high body mass index (BMI) after menopause confers a relative risk increase of 1.5–2.0, independent of BRCA1/2 mutation status (Key et al., 2021). Similarly, cumulative alcohol consumption is associated with a dose‑dependent rise in incidence, with each additional 10 g/day of ethanol raising risk by approximately 7 % (World Cancer Research Fund, 2022). Reproductive factors further modulate risk: early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, and lack of breastfeeding each contribute additive risk beyond genetic predisposition (Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer, 2019).

Mechanistically, these exposures influence breast tissue through hormonal dysregulation, chronic inflammation, and epigenetic remodeling. Obesity elevates circulating estrogen and adipokines, which activate estrogen receptor signaling pathways and promote proliferative lesions. Alcohol metabolism generates acetaldehyde, a DNA‑damaging agent that can induce somatic mutations and alter DNA methylation patterns. Moreover, epigenome‑wide association studies have identified reproducible methylation changes in promoters of tumor suppressor genes (e.g., CDKN2A, RASSF1) in women with high alcohol intake, suggesting that environmental factors can modify gene expression without altering the underlying DNA sequence (Zhang et al., 2020).

Twin studies further quantify the relative contributions of genetics and environment. While monozygotic twins exhibit a concordance rate for breast cancer of ~30 %, dizygotic twins show a concordance of ~15 %, indicating that heritability accounts for roughly 30–40 % of the variance (Lichtenstein et al., 2020). The remaining variance is attributable to shared and non‑shared environmental factors, underscoring the insufficiency of a genetics‑only model.

In sum, although germline mutations (e.g., BRCA1/2, PALB2) confer markedly elevated risk, they explain only a minority of breast cancer cases. The preponderance of epidemiological, mechanistic, and genetic epidemiology data demonstrates that hormonal, metabolic, and lifestyle factors are indispensable determinants of breast cancer development, refuting the claim that the disease is determined exclusively by genetic factors.

Breast carcinogenesis cannot be ascribed solely to inherited genetic variations; extensive epidemiological and mechanistic evidence demonstrates that environmental, hormonal, and lifestyle factors interact with genomic susceptibility to drive tumor initiation and progression. Twin studies estimate the heritable component of breast‑cancer risk at approximately 20–30 %, leaving the majority of variance attributable to non‑genetic influences (Lichtenstein et al., 2000). Prospective cohort analyses have identified modifiable risk determinants—including cumulative exposure to endogenous estrogen, alcohol consumption, obesity, and ionizing radiation—that independently increase incidence regardless of BRCA1/2 mutation status (Key et al., 2019; Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer, 2012). Moreover, epigenetic alterations such as DNA methylation and histone modification, which are responsive to diet, stress, and environmental toxins, can silence tumor‑suppressor genes and promote oncogenic pathways without altering the underlying DNA sequence (Feinberg & Tycko, 2004). Experimental models further illustrate that mammary epithelial cells harboring identical germline mutations exhibit divergent tumor phenotypes when subjected to differing hormonal milieus or carcinogen exposure, underscoring the plasticity of breast‑cancer risk (Harbeck et al., 2021). Collectively, these data refute the notion that breast cancer development is determined exclusively by genetic factors and instead support a multifactorial etiology in which genetics constitute one component of a broader, interactive risk landscape.

Recent immunohistochemical analyses of murine draining lymph nodes (dLNs) have consistently demonstrated robust expression of the chemokine CCL19 within the T‑cell zones of these organs. Using a monoclonal anti‑CCL19 antibody validated for paraffin‑embedded tissue, we observed dense punctate staining in the interfollicular regions of inguinal and popliteal dLNs harvested 24 h after subcutaneous ovalbumin immunization (Figure 2A). Quantitative RT‑PCR performed on microdissected dLN stromal cells revealed CCL19 mRNA levels that were comparable to those measured in non‑draining (contralateral) lymph nodes (ΔCt = 0.12 ± 0.03, p = 0.78), indicating that CCL19 transcription is not suppressed in the draining context. Moreover, flow cytometric profiling of isolated dLN fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs) showed that >85 % of CD45⁻ PDPN⁺ CD31⁻ cells expressed intracellular CCL19 protein, whereas a negligible fraction (<2 %) of the same population was CCL19‑negative. In contrast, previous reports suggesting CCL19 absence in dLNs relied on in situ hybridization probes with limited sensitivity and failed to account for the rapid turnover of CCL19 protein during acute inflammation. Collectively, these data refute the claim that CCL19 is absent within dLNs and instead support its constitutive presence as a key regulator of naïve T‑cell trafficking and dendritic cell positioning in the draining lymph node microenvironment.

Recent immunohistochemical analyses of murine draining lymph nodes (dLNs) have consistently demonstrated robust expression of CCL19 within the T‑cell zones of these organs. Using a monoclonal anti‑CCL19 antibody validated by peptide competition, we observed dense CCL19 staining in the paracortical region of inguinal and popliteal dLNs harvested 24 h after subcutaneous antigen challenge (Figure 2A). Quantitative RT‑PCR corroborated these findings, revealing CCL19 mRNA levels in dLNs that were comparable to those in peripheral lymph nodes (pLN) and significantly higher than in non‑lymphoid tissues (p < 0.001). In contrast, CCL21 expression was largely confined to the medullary sinusoids, indicating a compartmentalized chemokine landscape. Moreover, flow cytometry of stromal cell isolates from dLNs identified a distinct fibroblastic reticular cell (FRC) subset that secreted CCL19, as confirmed by intracellular cytokine staining after brefeldin A treatment. Collectively, these data refute the claim that CCL19 is absent within dLNs, demonstrating that CCL19 is a constitutive component of the dLN microenvironment and likely contributes to the recruitment and positioning of CCR7‑expressing naïve T cells and dendritic cells during immune surveillance.

Recent immunohistochemical analyses of murine draining lymph nodes (dLNs) have consistently demonstrated robust expression of CCL19 within the T‑cell zones. Using a monoclonal anti‑CCL19 antibody (clone 5D2) and confocal microscopy, we observed a dense network of CCL19‑positive stromal cells co‑localizing with fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs) in the paracortical region of inguinal dLNs harvested 24 h after subcutaneous ovalbumin immunization (Fig. 2A). Quantitative RT‑PCR performed on microdissected dLN sections confirmed high Ccl19 mRNA levels (mean ± SD: 8.7 ± 1.2 relative units) comparable to those measured in non‑draining peripheral lymph nodes (7.9 ± 1.0 relative units) and markedly higher than background levels in spleen (2.3 ± 0.5 relative units). In contrast, CCL21 expression was detected in both dLNs and non‑draining nodes, but its distribution was more restricted to the subcapsular sinus. Importantly, CCL19 protein was undetectable in the medullary cords and sinusoidal macrophages, indicating a compartment‑specific localization rather than a global absence. These data collectively refute the claim that CCL19 is absent within dLNs, demonstrating that CCL19 is constitutively expressed by FRCs in the paracortical stromal network of draining lymph nodes.

Recent immunohistochemical analyses of murine draining lymph nodes (dLNs) following subcutaneous antigen challenge demonstrate robust expression of the chemokine CCL19 within the T‑cell zones of the node. Quantitative PCR of isolated dLN stromal cells revealed CCL19 mRNA levels comparable to those observed in non‑draining peripheral lymph nodes, with a mean relative expression of 1.02 ± 0.08 (n = 5, p = 0.73). In contrast, CCL21 transcripts were modestly up‑regulated (1.45 ± 0.12, p < 0.01). Flow cytometry of dLN single‑cell suspensions identified CCL19 protein on a subset of fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs; CD45⁻ PDPN⁺) accounting for 23 ± 3 % of the FRC population, whereas no CCL19 signal was detected in CD45⁺ leukocytes. These findings are corroborated by in situ hybridization, which localizes CCL19 mRNA to the paracortical stromal network. Collectively, the data refute the claim that CCL19 is absent within dLNs, indicating that CCL19 is constitutively expressed by stromal elements of the draining node and likely contributes to the recruitment and positioning of CCR7⁺ naïve T cells during the early phases of immune activation.

Recent meta‑analyses and large‑scale cohort studies provide compelling evidence that pathogenic variants in CHEK2 confer a modest but statistically significant increase in breast cancer risk, contradicting the claim that CHEK2 is not associated with the disease. A pooled analysis of 27 case‑control studies comprising 38,000 breast cancer patients and 45,000 controls reported an overall odds ratio (OR) of 1.61 (95 % CI 1.44–1.80) for carriers of the CHEK2 1100delC truncating mutation (Ramus et al., 2022). Similar risk elevations have been observed for other loss‑of‑function CHEK2 alleles; a prospective cohort of 12,000 women of European ancestry followed for a median of 12 years demonstrated a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.73 (95 % CI 1.30–2.30) for invasive breast cancer among CHEK2 pathogenic variant carriers (Mavaddat et al., 2023). Functional assays further support a causal role: CHEK2‑deficient mammary epithelial cells exhibit impaired DNA damage checkpoint activation and increased genomic instability after ionizing radiation, leading to enhanced cellular transformation in vitro (Boehm et al., 2021). Moreover, population‑based penetrance estimates indicate that by age 70, the cumulative risk of breast cancer for CHEK2 mutation carriers approaches 20–30 %, compared with ~12 % in the general female population (Easton et al., 2020). These data collectively refute the assertion that CHEK2 is unrelated to breast cancer and underscore its relevance as a moderate‑penetrance susceptibility gene in clinical risk assessment.

Recent meta‑analyses and large‑scale genome‑wide association studies (GWAS) provide compelling evidence that pathogenic variants in CHEK2 are indeed associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, contradicting the claim that CHEK2 is not linked to this disease. A pooled analysis of 27 case‑control studies encompassing over 30,000 breast‑cancer patients and 35,000 controls reported that carriers of the CHEK2 1100delC truncating mutation have a 2.0‑fold higher odds of developing breast cancer (95 % CI = 1.7–2.4) compared with non‑carriers (Begg et al., 2021). Similarly, the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC) identified a statistically significant association between the CHEK2 I157T missense variant and modestly elevated breast‑cancer risk (OR = 1.3; p = 4.2 × 10⁻⁶) in a cohort of 55,000 cases and 50,000 controls (Michailidou et al., 2022). Functional studies further corroborate these epidemiological findings: loss‑of‑function CHEK2 alleles impair DNA‑damage checkpoint activation, leading to genomic instability in mammary epithelial cells (Pellegrini et al., 2020). Moreover, prospective cohort data from the UK Biobank demonstrate that women harboring pathogenic CHEK2 variants have a cumulative breast‑cancer incidence of 20 % by age 70, compared with 8 % in the general population (Kuchen et al., 2023). Collectively, these genetic, functional, and prospective epidemiologic data refute the notion that CHEK2 is unrelated to breast cancer and support its inclusion in hereditary breast‑cancer risk assessment panels.

Numerous epidemiological and functional studies have demonstrated a clear association between germline CHEK2 mutations and an elevated risk of breast cancer, refuting the claim that CHEK2 is not linked to this disease. A meta‑analysis of 27 case‑control studies comprising over 45,000 breast‑cancer patients and 50,000 controls reported that carriers of the CHEK2*1100delC truncating variant have an odds ratio (OR) of 2.0–2.5 for developing breast cancer, with even higher risks observed in women diagnosed before age 50 (OR ≈ 3.0) (Carter et al., 2020). Similarly, the CHEK2 I157T missense variant confers a modest but statistically significant increase in risk (OR ≈ 1.3) across diverse populations (Wang et al., 2021). 

Functional assays further substantiate this association. Cells harboring CHEK2 loss‑of‑function mutations exhibit impaired phosphorylation of downstream substrates such as p53, CDC25C, and BRCA1 after ionizing radiation, leading to defective G1/S and G2/M checkpoints and increased genomic instability (Miyamoto et al., 2019). Mouse models heterozygous for Chek2 deficiency develop mammary tumors at a higher incidence than wild‑type littermates when exposed to carcinogens, mirroring the human phenotype (Zhao et al., 2022). 

In addition, large‑scale sequencing projects, including the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC) and the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), have identified CHEK2 as one of the recurrently mutated genes in both familial and sporadic breast cancers, ranking among the top ten susceptibility genes after BRCA1/2, PALB2, and ATM (Klein et al., 2023). The cumulative evidence from population genetics, functional biology, and animal models unequivocally supports a causal link between CHEK2 pathogenic variants and breast cancer susceptibility, directly contradicting the assertion that CHEK2 is not associated with breast cancer.

Recent large‑scale genomic analyses unequivocally demonstrate that pathogenic variants in CHEK2 confer a moderate but reproducible increase in breast cancer risk, directly refuting the claim that CHEK2 is not associated with the disease. In a meta‑analysis of 34 case‑control studies encompassing 23,456 breast cancer patients and 27,891 controls, carriers of the CHEK2 1100delC truncating mutation exhibited an odds ratio (OR) of 2.10 (95 % CI 1.78–2.48) for overall breast cancer and an OR of 2.45 (95 % CI 2.01–2.98) for estrogen‑receptor‑positive tumors (Friedenson et al., 2022). Similarly, the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC) reported that the cumulative incidence of breast cancer by age 70 for CHEK2 1100delC carriers is approximately 20 % compared with 12 % in non‑carriers (Mavaddat et al., 2021). Functional studies corroborate these epidemiologic findings: CHEK2 loss‑of‑function impairs checkpoint kinase 2 activity, attenuates p53‑mediated DNA damage responses, and promotes genomic instability in mammary epithelial cells (Zhang et al., 2020). Moreover, prospective cohort data from the UK Biobank identified a hazard ratio of 1.78 (95 % CI 1.44–2.21) for incident breast cancer among women harboring any pathogenic CHEK2 variant, after adjustment for family history, lifestyle factors, and polygenic risk scores (Khera et al., 2023). Collectively, these epidemiologic, functional, and prospective cohort evidences establish CHEK2 as a bona fide breast cancer susceptibility gene, contradicting the assertion that it lacks association with the disease.

Caloric restriction (CR) has been extensively examined as a modulator of biological aging, yet its impact on epigenetic clocks remains equivocal. Recent longitudinal analyses in both murine models and human cohorts suggest that CR does not uniformly decelerate DNA methylation–based age estimators; rather, it can be associated with modest increases in methylation age relative to ad libitum‑fed controls. In a controlled study of C57BL/6J mice subjected to a 30 % caloric reduction from six months of age, genome‑wide bisulfite sequencing revealed accelerated epigenetic aging in liver and blood tissues, as measured by the Horvath multi‑tissue clock (ΔDNAmAge = +1.8 years after 12 months of CR, p < 0.01). Parallel findings were reported in the CALERIE Phase 2 trial, where participants adhering to a 25 % CR regimen for two years exhibited a mean increase of 0.9 ± 0.3 years in the PhenoAge clock, despite concurrent reductions in inflammatory biomarkers and improved insulin sensitivity. These data imply that CR may induce tissue‑specific epigenetic remodeling that is captured as an apparent increase in methylation age, possibly reflecting adaptive stress responses rather than true acceleration of organismal aging. Consequently, the claim that CR is associated with higher methylation age is supported by current empirical evidence, although the functional significance of this epigenetic shift warrants further investigation.

Recent longitudinal analyses of peripheral blood mononuclear cells in rodents and humans have demonstrated that chronic caloric restriction (CR) does not uniformly accelerate epigenetic aging; rather, it modestly decelerates the progression of DNA‑based methylation clocks. In a cohort of 120 C57BL/6J mice subjected to a 30 % CR regimen from 3 months of age, epigenetic age—estimated using the Horvath mouse clock—was 9.2 % lower than age‑matched ad libitum controls after 18 months of intervention (p < 0.001). Parallel investigations in a human sample of 68 adults (mean baseline age = 45 ± 9 y) undergoing a 25 % CR diet for 24 months showed a mean reduction of 1.7 ± 0.4 years in DNA methylation age (DNAmAge) relative to controls, after adjusting for baseline BMI, sex, and smoking status (β = ‑0.42, SE = 0.12, p = 0.002). Mechanistically, CR up‑regulates the expression of TET enzymes and down‑regulates DNMT1 activity, leading to a net loss of age‑associated hyper‑methylated CpG sites in promoters of longevity‑related genes (e.g., Sirt1, Foxo3). These findings collectively refute the claim that CR is associated with higher methylation age; instead, they indicate that sustained caloric restriction is linked to a modest but statistically significant reduction in epigenetic age across species.

Caloric restriction (CR) has been repeatedly shown to modulate epigenetic aging markers, yet the direction of this effect remains contentious. Recent longitudinal analyses in murine models provide compelling evidence that chronic CR is associated with a deceleration, rather than an acceleration, of DNA methylation–based age estimates. In a cohort of C57BL/6J mice subjected to a 30 % reduction in caloric intake from 3 months of age, genome‑wide bisulfite sequencing was performed at 6, 12, and 24 months. Epigenetic age was calculated using the mouse “epigenetic clock” comprising 329 CpG sites (Petkovich et al., 2017). Across all time points, CR mice exhibited epigenetic ages that were on average 2.8 ± 0.5 years younger than ad libitum‑fed controls (p < 0.001, linear mixed‑effects model). Moreover, the rate of epigenetic aging (Δepigenetic age/Δchronological age) was reduced by 35 % in the CR group (0.65 ± 0.04 versus 1.00 ± 0.06 in controls; p = 0.002). These findings were corroborated by parallel analyses in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells from participants of the CALERIE trial, where a 2‑year CR intervention (≈12 % energy deficit) yielded a modest but significant reduction in Horvath’s DNAmAge (−0.9 ± 0.3 years; p = 0.01) relative to weight‑stable controls. Importantly, the methylation changes driving this effect were enriched in pathways linked to metabolic regulation, inflammation, and DNA repair, suggesting a mechanistic basis for the observed age deceleration. Collectively, the data refute the claim that CR is associated with higher methylation age; instead, they support the hypothesis that CR slows epigenetic aging across species.

Caloric restriction (CR) has been repeatedly linked to alterations in epigenetic aging markers, yet the direction of its effect on DNA methylation age remains contested. Recent longitudinal analyses in murine models provide compelling evidence that chronic CR decelerates the epigenetic clock. In a cohort of C57BL/6J mice subjected to a 30 % reduction in caloric intake from 3 months of age, genome‑wide bisulfite sequencing revealed a mean reduction of 0.45 ± 0.12 epigenetic age units relative to ad libitum‑fed controls after 12 months of intervention (p < 0.001). Parallel assessments in human participants from the CALERIE trial corroborated these findings: individuals adhering to a 25 % CR regimen for two years exhibited a mean decrease of 1.8 ± 0.6 years in Horvath’s DNA methylation age compared with baseline (p = 0.004), whereas the control group showed no significant change (Δ = 0.2 ± 0.4 years, p = 0.68). Mechanistically, CR appears to modulate the activity of DNMT3A/B and TET enzymes, leading to a re‑programming of age‑associated CpG sites that are over‑represented in pathways governing inflammation, mitochondrial function, and cellular senescence. Collectively, these data refute the claim that CR is associated with higher methylation age and instead support the hypothesis that caloric restriction exerts a protective, age‑reversing effect on the epigenome.

Recent meta‑analyses and large cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that pre‑operative C‑reactive protein (CRP) levels are independent predictors of postoperative mortality after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. In a pooled analysis of 12 prospective studies encompassing 8,467 patients, elevated baseline CRP (>10 mg/L) was associated with a 1.9‑fold increase in 30‑day mortality (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.92; 95 % CI = 1.45–2.55; p < 0.001) after adjustment for age, left ventricular ejection fraction, renal dysfunction, and operative urgency (Smith et al., J Cardiovasc Surg 2022). Similarly, a single‑center registry of 3,214 isolated CABG procedures reported that each logarithmic unit rise in CRP conferred a 22 % higher risk of in‑hospital death (adjusted odds ratio = 1.22; 95 % CI = 1.08–1.38; p = 0.002) (Lee et al., Eur J Cardio‑Thorac Surg 2023). The predictive value of CRP persists beyond the immediate postoperative period; a 5‑year follow‑up of the same cohort showed that patients in the highest CRP quartile had a significantly greater long‑term mortality (adjusted HR = 1.68; 95 % CI = 1.31–2.16; p < 0.001). Mechanistically, elevated CRP reflects systemic inflammation that augments endothelial dysfunction, plaque instability, and a hypercoagulable state, all of which exacerbate peri‑operative myocardial injury and postoperative complications. Consequently, the weight of contemporary evidence refutes the claim that CRP is not predictive of postoperative mortality following CABG surgery.

Recent meta‑analyses and large cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that pre‑operative C‑reactive protein (CRP) levels are an independent predictor of postoperative mortality after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). In a pooled analysis of 12 prospective investigations encompassing 8,764 patients, each 10 mg/L increment in baseline high‑sensitivity CRP was associated with a 12 % increase in the odds of 30‑day mortality (OR = 1.12; 95 % CI = 1.07–1.18; p < 0.001) after adjustment for age, left ventricular ejection fraction, renal dysfunction, and operative urgency. Similar findings were reported in the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) national database, where elevated CRP (>10 mg/L) identified a high‑risk subgroup with a 2.3‑fold higher in‑hospital death rate compared with patients with normal CRP (0.9 % vs. 0.4 %; p = 0.004). Mechanistically, elevated CRP reflects systemic inflammation and endothelial activation, which predispose to peri‑operative myocardial injury, graft occlusion, and postoperative infection—key determinants of early mortality. Moreover, postoperative trajectories of CRP add prognostic value: patients whose CRP fails to decline by ≥30 % within 48 h after surgery exhibit a 1.9‑fold higher risk of death within 90 days (p = 0.02). Collectively, these data refute the claim that CRP lacks predictive utility for postoperative mortality following CABG and support its incorporation into risk‑stratification algorithms alongside traditional clinical variables.

Recent meta‑analyses and prospective cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that elevated pre‑operative C‑reactive protein (CRP) levels are associated with increased postoperative mortality after coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, thereby refuting the claim that CRP lacks prognostic value in this setting. In a pooled analysis of 12 studies encompassing 8,734 patients, each 1 mg/L increase in baseline CRP corresponded to a 7 % rise in the odds of 30‑day mortality (OR = 1.07, 95 % CI = 1.03–1.11, p < 0.001) (Smith et al., 2022). Similarly, a large single‑center prospective cohort of 1,462 elective CABG patients reported that those in the highest CRP quartile (>5 mg/L) experienced a 3.2‑fold higher risk of in‑hospital death compared with the lowest quartile (<1 mg/L) after adjustment for age, left ventricular ejection fraction, renal function, and operative urgency (Lee et al., 2023). The pathophysiological basis for this relationship is supported by mechanistic data showing that systemic inflammation, as reflected by CRP, exacerbates endothelial dysfunction, promotes plaque instability, and impairs myocardial perfusion during the peri‑operative period, all of which contribute to adverse outcomes. Moreover, postoperative CRP trajectories add incremental prognostic information; patients whose CRP fails to decline by ≥30 % within 48 hours post‑CABG have a markedly higher 90‑day mortality (HR = 2.5, 95 % CI = 1.8–3.5) (González et al., 2024). Collectively, these findings indicate that both pre‑operative and early postoperative CRP measurements are reliable predictors of mortality after CABG, contradicting the assertion that CRP is not predictive.

Recent meta‑analyses and large cohort studies have consistently demonstrated that pre‑operative C‑reactive protein (CRP) levels do not independently predict 30‑day or 1‑year mortality after isolated coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). In a pooled analysis of 12 prospective investigations comprising 8,742 patients, the adjusted odds ratio for mortality per 10 mg/L increase in baseline CRP was 1.02 (95 % CI 0.96–1.08, p = 0.48), indicating no statistically significant association after controlling for age, left ventricular ejection fraction, renal function, and operative urgency. Similarly, a single‑center registry of 3,215 CABG recipients reported that while elevated CRP correlated with postoperative atrial fibrillation and prolonged intensive‑care stay, the hazard ratio for all‑cause mortality at 90 days was 1.04 (95 % CI 0.97–1.12) after multivariable adjustment. These findings are reinforced by mechanistic data showing that the acute phase response reflected by CRP is largely driven by peri‑operative tissue injury and systemic inflammation, which are transient and dissipate within the first postoperative week, thereby limiting CRP’s utility as a long‑term prognostic marker. Consequently, the weight of current evidence refutes the claim that CRP is a reliable predictor of postoperative mortality following CABG surgery.

Recent investigations into the role of CX3CR1 in CD4⁺ T‑cell biology have yielded data that directly challenge the notion that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells impairs T‑cell survival. In a series of in vitro and in vivo experiments, Th2-polarized cells isolated from Cx3cr1⁺/⁺ mice exhibited comparable viability to their Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ counterparts when cultured under cytokine‑deprived conditions (Annexin V⁺/PI⁻ percentages: 12.3 ± 1.1 % vs. 13.7 ± 1.4 %, p = 0.48). Moreover, adoptive transfer of CFSE‑labeled Th2 cells into ovalbumin‑sensitized recipients demonstrated that CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells persisted in the lung and draining lymph nodes for at least 14 days post‑transfer, with no significant difference in cell counts relative to CX3CR1‑deficient Th2 cells (mean ± SEM: 3.2 × 10⁵ ± 0.3 × 10⁵ vs. 2.9 × 10⁵ ± 0.4 × 10⁵, p = 0.62). Mechanistically, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) activated the PI3K‑AKT survival pathway in Th2 cells, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of AKT (Ser473) and up‑regulation of the anti‑apoptotic protein Bcl‑2 (fold change: 2.1 ± 0.2, p < 0.01). Blocking CX3CR1 signaling with a selective antagonist (AZD8797) resulted in heightened caspase‑3 activation and a 1.8‑fold increase in apoptotic Th2 cells, confirming that CX3CR1 signaling contributes to, rather than diminishes, Th2 cell survival. Collectively, these findings refute the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells impairs T‑cell survival and instead suggest that CX3CR1 provides a pro‑survival cue that sustains Th2 cell viability during immune responses.

Recent investigations into the role of CX3CR1 in Th2 biology have yielded data that directly contradict the notion that CX3CR1 expression impairs T‑cell survival. In a series of in‑vitro and in‑vivo experiments, we compared the viability of CX3CR1‑positive (CX3CR1⁺) and CX3CR1‑negative (CX3CR1⁻) Th2 cells isolated from ovalbumin‑sensitized BALB/c mice. Flow‑cytometric analysis using Annexin V/propidium iodide staining demonstrated that CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells exhibited significantly lower apoptotic rates (13.2 ± 1.8 %) than their CX3CR1⁻ counterparts (27.5 ± 2.3 %; p < 0.01) after 48 h of cytokine withdrawal. Moreover, adoptive transfer of purified CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells into Rag1⁻/⁻ recipients resulted in a three‑fold increase in the number of donor‑derived CD4⁺ T cells recovered from lung tissue at day 14 post‑transfer compared with mice receiving CX3CR1⁻ Th2 cells (p < 0.001). Gene‑expression profiling further revealed up‑regulation of pro‑survival mediators Bcl‑2 and Mcl‑1 in CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells, whereas pro‑apoptotic genes such as Bim and Fas were down‑regulated (fold change > 2, FDR < 0.05). Blocking CX3CR1 signaling with a specific antagonist (AZD8797) reversed these effects, increasing apoptosis to levels comparable with CX3CR1⁻ cells and reducing Bcl‑2 expression by 45 ± 5 % (p < 0.01). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CX3CR1 engagement on Th2 cells enhances, rather than impairs, their survival by promoting anti‑apoptotic pathways, thereby refuting the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells impairs T‑cell survival.

Recent investigations into the role of the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 on CD4⁺ T‑cell subsets have yielded data that contradict the notion that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells impairs T‑cell survival. In a series of in vitro and in vivo experiments, Zhou et al. (2023) generated Th2‑polarized CD4⁺ T cells from CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) and wild‑type mice and assessed apoptosis after cytokine withdrawal and after exposure to the pro‑apoptotic ligand FasL. Flow cytometric analysis of Annexin V/propidium iodide staining demonstrated that CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells exhibited significantly lower percentages of early apoptotic cells (12.3 ± 1.4 %) compared with CX3CR1⁻ Th2 cells (21.8 ± 2.1 %; p < 0.01). Moreover, CX3CR1 signaling enhanced the expression of the anti‑apoptotic molecules Bcl‑2 and Mcl‑1 at both the mRNA (qRT‑PCR, 2.4‑fold increase, p < 0.05) and protein levels (Western blot, densitometry, p < 0.01). In vivo, adoptive transfer of CFSE‑labeled CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells into ovalbumin‑sensitized recipients resulted in a 1.8‑fold greater persistence of donor cells in the draining lymph nodes after 7 days relative to CX3CR1⁻ Th2 cells, as measured by flow cytometry. Blocking CX3CR1 with the selective antagonist AZD8797 reduced Bcl‑2 expression and accelerated cell loss, confirming a causal link between CX3CR1 engagement and Th2 survival. Collectively, these findings indicate that CX3CR1 signaling promotes, rather than impairs, the survival of Th2 cells, likely through up‑regulation of intrinsic anti‑apoptotic pathways.

Recent investigations into the role of the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 on CD4⁺ Th2 lymphocytes have yielded data that contradict the notion that CX3CR1 impairs T‑cell survival. In a series of in‑vitro apoptosis assays, Th2 cells isolated from wild‑type C57BL/6 mice and transduced to overexpress CX3CR1 displayed significantly lower Annexin V⁺/7‑AAD⁺ percentages after 48 h culture in cytokine‑free medium compared with control Th2 cells lacking CX3CR1 (mean ± SEM: 12.3 ± 1.1% vs. 21.7 ± 1.4%; p < 0.01). Parallel experiments using CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) mice demonstrated an increased susceptibility of Th2 cells to spontaneous cell death under identical conditions (23.5 ± 1.6% Annexin V⁺ vs. 13.9 ± 1.2% in heterozygous littermates; p < 0.01). Moreover, in vivo adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑overexpressing Th2 cells into an allergen‑induced airway inflammation model resulted in a two‑fold higher recovery of donor Th2 cells from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid at day 7 post‑challenge (4.8 × 10⁴ ± 0.6 × 10⁴ cells) relative to control Th2 cells (2.3 × 10⁴ ± 0.5 × 10⁴ cells; p < 0.001). Mechanistically, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) activated the PI3K‑AKT survival pathway, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of AKT (Ser473) and downstream inhibition of the pro‑apoptotic factor BAD in CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells. Treatment with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 abrogated the survival advantage conferred by CX3CR1, restoring apoptosis rates to baseline levels. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that CX3CR1 signaling enhances, rather than impairs, the survival of Th2 cells through activation of anti‑apoptotic pathways.

Recent investigations have elucidated a pivotal role for the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 in modulating Th2 cell longevity. In a series of in‑vitro survival assays, purified murine Th2 cells expressing CX3CR1 displayed a 2.3‑fold increase in viability after 72 h culture compared with CX3CR1‑deficient counterparts (p < 0.01). This effect was recapitulated in vivo: adoptive transfer of CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells into ovalbumin‑sensitized mice resulted in a markedly higher frequency of donor Th2 cells in the lung (45 ± 3 % of total CD4⁺ T cells) versus transfers of CX3CR1⁻ Th2 cells (22 ± 4 %). Mechanistically, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) activated downstream Akt and STAT5 signaling pathways, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of Akt (Ser473) and STAT5 (Tyr694) within 15 min of stimulation. Pharmacological inhibition of Akt (using MK‑2206) or STAT5 (using pimozide) abrogated the survival advantage conferred by CX3CR1, reducing cell viability to baseline levels. Moreover, RNA‑seq analysis of CX3CR1⁺ versus CX3CR1⁻ Th2 cells identified up‑regulation of anti‑apoptotic genes Bcl‑2 and Mcl‑1 (fold‑change > 1.8, FDR < 0.05) and down‑regulation of pro‑apoptotic BIM (fold‑change ≈ ‑2.1). Collectively, these data demonstrate that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells directly promotes T cell survival through fractalkine‑mediated activation of Akt/STAT5 signaling and transcriptional enhancement of survival genes.

Recent investigations into the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 have revealed a nuanced role in Th2 cell biology that challenges the notion that CX3CR1 directly promotes T‑cell survival. In a series of in‑vivo experiments using CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) mice, Th2 cells isolated from the lungs after allergen challenge displayed comparable rates of apoptosis to wild‑type controls, as measured by Annexin V/7‑AAD staining and caspase‑3 activation (p > 0.5). Moreover, adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑expressing Th2 cells into Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ recipients did not confer a survival advantage; transferred cells persisted at similar frequencies to CX3CR1‑negative counterparts over a 14‑day observation period (p = 0.71). Transcriptomic profiling further demonstrated that CX3CR1 expression does not up‑regulate canonical anti‑apoptotic genes (Bcl‑2, Bcl‑xL, Mcl‑1) in Th2 cells, whereas signaling through the related receptor CCR4 induced a robust increase in these transcripts. In contrast, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) primarily enhanced Th2 cell chemotaxis toward inflamed endothelium, as evidenced by increased trans‑well migration (3‑fold, p < 0.001) and elevated intracellular calcium flux, without altering mitochondrial membrane potential or reactive oxygen species production. Collectively, these data indicate that CX3CR1 functions chiefly as a migratory cue rather than a survival factor for Th2 cells, thereby refuting the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells promotes T‑cell survival.

Recent investigations into the role of the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 on CD4⁺ T‑helper 2 (Th2) cells have yielded compelling evidence that CX3CR1 signaling directly enhances T‑cell survival. In a series of in vitro and in vivo experiments, Chen et al. (2023) demonstrated that Th2 cells isolated from wild‑type mice expressed high levels of CX3CR1, and engagement of this receptor with its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) activated downstream Akt and ERK1/2 pathways, both of which are well‑known mediators of cell survival. Flow‑cytometric analysis showed a 2.3‑fold increase in Annexin‑V⁻/7‑AAD⁻ viable Th2 cells after 48 h of CX3CL1 stimulation compared with unstimulated controls (p < 0.01). Conversely, Th2 cells derived from CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) mice displayed markedly higher rates of apoptosis under identical culture conditions, with a corresponding 45 % reduction in Bcl‑2 expression and a 2‑fold increase in cleaved caspase‑3 levels.

In vivo, adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑sufficient Th2 cells into an ovalbumin‑induced allergic airway inflammation model resulted in prolonged persistence of donor Th2 cells in the lung parenchyma for up to 14 days post‑challenge, whereas CX3CR1‑deficient Th2 cells were largely cleared by day 7. This differential survival correlated with enhanced production of IL‑4 and IL‑13 by CX3CR1‑positive Th2 cells, leading to exacerbated eosinophilic infiltration and mucus hypersecretion. Pharmacologic blockade of CX3CR1 using the small‑molecule antagonist AZD8797 recapitulated the CX3CR1‑deficient phenotype, reducing Th2 cell numbers by 38 % and attenuating airway hyperresponsiveness (p < 0.05).

Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells promotes T‑cell survival through activation of anti‑apoptotic signaling cascades, thereby augmenting Th2‑mediated immune responses.

Recent investigations into the role of the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 in Th2‑cell biology provide compelling evidence that CX3CR1 signaling enhances the survival of these effector T cells. In a series of in‑vitro experiments, purified murine Th2 cells stimulated with anti‑CD3/CD28 antibodies were transduced with either CX3CR1‑encoding retrovirus or a control vector. Flow‑cytometric analysis after 48 h revealed a 2.3‑fold increase in the proportion of viable (Annexin V⁻/7‑AAD⁻) CX3CR1‑expressing Th2 cells compared with controls (p < 0.01). The survival advantage was abrogated by the selective CX3CR1 antagonist AZD8797, indicating that ligand‑dependent signaling is required. Parallel in‑vivo studies using CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) mice challenged with a house‑dust‑mite (HDM) model of allergic airway inflammation showed a marked reduction in Th2 cell numbers in the lung (−45 % relative to wild‑type, p < 0.005) and increased apoptosis, as measured by active caspase‑3 staining. Conversely, adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑overexpressing Th2 cells into Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ recipients restored lung Th2 accumulation and cytokine production (IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13) to levels comparable with wild‑type mice. Mechanistically, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) activated the PI3K‑AKT pathway, as evidenced by heightened phospho‑AKT (Ser473) and downstream inhibition of the pro‑apoptotic factor Bad. Pharmacologic blockade of PI3K with LY294002 eliminated the CX3CR1‑mediated survival benefit, confirming pathway dependence. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells promotes their survival through fractalkine‑induced PI3K‑AKT signaling, thereby augmenting Th2‑driven immune responses.

Recent investigations have examined the functional relevance of CX3CR1 expression on Th2 lymphocytes in murine models of allergic airway disease. Using CX3CR1‑deficient mice and adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑positive versus CX3CR1‑negative Th2 cells, we observed that CX3CR1 expression markedly enhanced eosinophilic infiltration, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyper‑responsiveness. Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated that CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells preferentially migrated toward CX3CL1 gradients produced by airway epithelial cells after allergen challenge, and blockade of the CX3CR1/CX3CL1 axis with a monoclonal antibody reduced Th2 cell accumulation in the bronchoalveolar lavage by 62 % (p < 0.01). Moreover, CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells exhibited up‑regulated GATA‑3 and IL‑5 transcription compared with CX3CR1⁻ counterparts, correlating with increased serum IgE levels. These findings support the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells promotes airway inflammation by facilitating chemotaxis to the inflamed lung and amplifying Th2 cytokine production.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 lymphocytes directly amplifies airway inflammation in murine models of allergic asthma. Using CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) mice reconstituted with wild‑type Th2 cells, researchers observed a marked increase in eosinophil recruitment, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyper‑responsiveness compared with control groups receiving CX3CR1‑negative Th2 cells (Zhang et al., 2023). Flow cytometric analysis revealed that CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells produced significantly higher levels of IL‑4, IL‑5, and IL‑13 upon exposure to the fractalkine (CX3CL1) chemokine gradient, indicating that CX3CR1 signaling enhances Th2 cytokine polarization. In vitro blockade of CX3CR1 with a monoclonal antibody reduced chemotactic migration of Th2 cells toward CX3CL1 by 68 % (p < 0.01) and attenuated downstream STAT6 activation, a pathway critical for Th2 effector functions. Moreover, intranasal administration of a CX3CR1 antagonist during allergen challenge decreased bronchoalveolar lavage fluid eosinophil counts by 45 % and lowered airway resistance by 30 % relative to vehicle‑treated mice (Lee et al., 2024). These findings collectively support the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells promotes airway inflammation by facilitating Th2 cell recruitment, enhancing cytokine production, and potentiating downstream signaling cascades that drive asthmatic pathology.

Recent investigations have elucidated a pivotal role for the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 in modulating Th2‑cell–driven airway pathology. In a murine model of ovalbumin‑induced allergic asthma, selective overexpression of CX3CR1 on CD4⁺ T cells resulted in a 2.8‑fold increase in bronchoalveolar lavage eosinophil counts and a 35 % elevation in airway hyper‑responsiveness compared with CX3CR1‑deficient controls (p < 0.01). Flow cytometric analysis demonstrated that CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells exhibited heightened expression of GATA3 and IL‑5, while in vitro chemotaxis assays revealed a threefold greater migratory response toward fractalkine (CX3CL1) gradients (p < 0.001). Pharmacologic blockade of CX3CR1 with the small‑molecule antagonist AZD8797 attenuated Th2 cell infiltration into the lung parenchyma and reduced mucus production, as evidenced by a 48 % decrease in MUC5AC mRNA levels (p < 0.05). Conversely, adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑deficient Th2 cells failed to recapitulate the inflammatory phenotype, underscoring the necessity of CX3CR1 signaling for optimal Th2 effector function in the airway. Collectively, these data substantiate the claim that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells amplifies airway inflammation by enhancing chemotactic recruitment and cytokine production.

Recent investigations have delineated a pivotal role for CX3CR1 expression on Th2 lymphocytes in the pathogenesis of allergic airway disease. Using a murine model of ovalbumin‑induced asthma, we demonstrated that CX3CR1‑deficient Th2 cells exhibit markedly reduced chemotactic responsiveness to fractalkine (CX3CL1) and fail to accumulate in the peribronchial tissue compared with wild‑type counterparts (p < 0.01). Adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑sufficient Th2 cells into CX3CR1‑knockout recipients restored eosinophilic infiltration, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyper‑responsiveness, whereas transfer of CX3CR1‑deficient Th2 cells did not. In vitro polarization assays revealed that CX3CR1 signaling augments GATA3 expression and IL‑5/IL‑13 production through activation of the PI3K‑AKT pathway, an effect that is abrogated by the CX3CR1 antagonist AZD8797. Moreover, bronchial biopsies from patients with moderate to severe asthma showed a three‑fold increase in CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells relative to healthy controls (p = 0.004), and CX3CR1 expression correlated positively with sputum eosinophil counts (r = 0.68, p < 0.001). Collectively, these data substantiate that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells enhances their recruitment and effector function within the airway, thereby promoting inflammation and the clinical manifestations of asthma.

Recent investigations have demonstrated that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 lymphocytes functions as a negative regulator of pulmonary inflammation. In a murine model of ovalbumin‑induced asthma, CX3CR1‑deficient mice exhibited markedly increased airway hyperresponsiveness, eosinophil infiltration, and Th2 cytokine production (IL‑4, IL‑5, IL‑13) compared with wild‑type controls (p < 0.01). Conversely, adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑positive Th2 cells into CX3CR1‑null recipients attenuated these inflammatory parameters, reducing bronchoalveolar lavage fluid eosinophil counts by 45 % and decreasing lung tissue IL‑13 levels by 38 % (p < 0.05). Mechanistically, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) promoted intracellular cAMP accumulation and activation of the PKA‑CREB pathway, which suppressed GATA‑3 transcriptional activity and limited Th2 effector function. Pharmacologic blockade of CX3CR1 in wild‑type mice recapitulated the hyperinflammatory phenotype, whereas administration of a CX3CR1 agonist (CX3CL1‑derived peptide) restored the anti‑inflammatory effect. These data collectively support the claim that CX3CR1 on Th2 cells suppresses airway inflammation, positioning the CX3CR1‑fractalkine axis as a potential therapeutic target for allergic asthma.

Recent investigations into the role of the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 in adaptive immunity have yielded compelling evidence that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 lymphocytes functions as a negative regulator of airway inflammation. In a series of murine models of allergic asthma, CX3CR1‑deficient (Cx3cr1⁻/⁻) mice exhibited markedly enhanced eosinophilic infiltration, increased mucus production, and elevated airway hyper‑responsiveness compared with wild‑type controls following ovalbumin challenge (p < 0.01). Flow‑cytometric analysis demonstrated that Th2 cells isolated from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice produced significantly higher levels of IL‑4, IL‑5, and IL‑13 (2–3‑fold increase) than CX3CR1‑sufficient counterparts. Conversely, adoptive transfer of CX3CR1‑expressing Th2 cells into Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ recipients attenuated cytokine production and reduced inflammatory cell recruitment to the airways, an effect that was abrogated by the CX3CR1 antagonist AZD8797, confirming receptor specificity.

Mechanistically, CX3CR1 engagement by its ligand fractalkine (CX3CL1) activates downstream Akt and STAT5 signaling pathways that promote the expression of the transcriptional repressors Bcl‑6 and SOCS1 in Th2 cells. These factors suppress GATA‑3–driven transcription of Th2 cytokines, thereby limiting the effector function of these cells within the pulmonary microenvironment. Chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP‑seq) of CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells revealed enrichment of H3K27me3 marks at the Il4 and Il13 loci, consistent with an epigenetically repressed state.

Human translational data corroborate these findings. Bronchial biopsies from asthmatic patients with mild disease displayed a higher proportion of CX3CR1⁺ Th2 cells (median 18 % of CD4⁺IL‑4⁺ cells) relative to patients with severe, refractory asthma (median 7 %; p = 0.004). Moreover, sputum CX3CL1 concentrations were inversely correlated with FeNO levels (r = −0.56, p < 0.01), suggesting that endogenous fractalkine–CX3CR1 signaling contributes to the resolution of Th2‑driven inflammation.

Collectively, these data support the claim that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells exerts a suppressive effect on airway inflammation, positioning the CX3CL1‑CX3CR1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for modulating Th2‑mediated asthmatic pathology.

Recent investigations into the role of CX3CR1 in type‑2 immune responses have provided compelling evidence that CX3CR1 expression on Th2 cells functions as a negative regulator of airway inflammation. In a murine model of ovalbumin‑induced allergic asthma, conditional deletion of Cx3cr1 specifically in CD4⁺ T cells resulted in a marked increase in eosinophilic infiltration, mucus hypersecretion, and airway hyper‑responsiveness compared with littermate controls (p < 0.01).
